entries.text: Before you can design a dress, you need to <style=c1>measure</style> your client.
<style=c1>Drag the measuring tape</style> onto the client's body to take measurements.
Move the tape to measure the <style=c1>bust</style>, <style=c1>waist</style>, and <style=c1>hips</style>. Hold still for a moment to record each measurement.
All measurements recorded! Click <style=c1>Confirm</style> to accept the commission.
Now you need to <style=c1>adjust the mannequin</style> to match your client's measurements.
<style=c1>Drag the measuring tape</style> onto the mannequin.
<style=c1>Turn the gears</style> to adjust the mannequin's proportions. Match the ghost outlines for the best fit.
Great fit! Click <style=c1>Confirm</style> when you're satisfied with the mannequin sizing.
Every dress starts with a design in your sketchbook.
Your <color=#0e85d9>style</color>, choice of <color=#0e85d9>fabric</color>, and overall <color=#0e85d9>execution</color> determine how happy your client will be.
Change your design by <style=c1>clicking the arrows</style> next to each component.
You can also save fabric and haberdashery samples in the sketchbook.
<style=c1>Drag fabric</style> onto the page to test how your design and fabric fit the client's needs.
These tags are just an estimate! The real fabric used affects the final result.
Use the <style=c1>pencil</style> to try colour combos.
Now find a <style=c1>design</style> and <style=c1>fabric</style> that is appropriate for a <color=#0e85d9>Professional</color> garment.
When you are happy with your design, click <color=#0e85d9>Draft Pattern</color>.
Here you can buy more fabric to use for making dresses.
You should try <style=c1>buy fabrics</style> appropriate to your client's desires - try and find ones that are tagged as <style=c1>professional</style>.
You can <style=c1>filter</style> the available options by clicking the filter button.
Get at least <style=c1>5 meters</style> of fabric... just to be safe. You can always use it later!
Nice choices! You may continue shopping and <style=c1>return to the front desk</style> when ready.
Select the fabric you'd like to use by clicking on it in the sidebar.
To begin cutting, switch to <color=#0e85d9>patterns</color> on the sidebar.
<color=#0e85d9>Drag</color> your pattern pieces onto the fabric to begin cutting.
Aligning the <style=c1>grain</style> line <style=c1>horizontally</style> will result in a higher <style=c1>quality</style> garment.
Use the <style=c1>rotation knob</style> to rotate the pattern piece so it aligns with the horizontal grain line
Now select the <color=#0e85d9>scissors</color> and click on the pattern piece to cut it out.
You can always recut or dispose if you are unhappy - you will get back the piece of fabric you used!
Now <color=#0e85d9>right click</color> or <color=#0e85d9>drag</color> the piece back into your inventory.
Great! Now place, align and cut out the rest of the pieces of the fabric.

You can discard used parts of your fabric to make space for more pieces by pressing the <color=#0e85d9>discard fabric button</color> or holding the <color=#0e85d9>scissors</color> at the top or bottom edge of the roll, then clicking.
Oops! It seems like you've run out of fabric. It's important to remain efficient with usage! For now, have some extra, on the house!
Now you may drag the pieces back into your inventory and return to the <color=#0e85d9>front desk</color>.
You may now <style=c1>assemble</style> and assess your dress on the mannequin.
<style=c1>Drag the cut out fabric pieces</style> from your inventory onto the appropriate spot on the mannequin.
If you are happy with the layout of the pieces, you can sew them together by clicking the <color=#0e85d9>sew</color> button.
Great! Now complete the rest of the pieces.
Remember, you can always remove a panel, return to the cutting room and cut it again!
Congratulations! You've completed your first dress!
Now we'll sew this piece to its neighbour.
<style=c1>Drag the mouse</style> left and right to rotate the piece.
We've unlocked some <style=c1>Accessories</style>, let's buy some!
Let's add some <style=c1>accessories</style> to this dress.
Click to select an accessory piece, and click on where you want to position it on the dress.
You can drag the items to rearrange, or drag them back to the inventory to remove.
Before returning the dress to our customer, let's take a photo for our records.
Adjust camera angle with the <style=c1>Camera Controls</style>
You can also adjust the environment with the environmental controls.
When you are happy with your shot, click <style=c1>Take Photo</style>.
You can now also make off the rack dresses which you can sell for extra income and prestige!
Click the <style=c1>non commissioned dress</style> tab to start.
You may now also gift dresses to the clients you've met. Each client has their own preferences and measurements, you can see these in the Sketchbook.

The Office of the Crown of Queen Sophie Vasar of Hemstitch has received word of your great accomplishments and service to the town of Twillford. By our estimations and observations, we deem you to be an outstanding artisan, worthy of national recognition. We also understand you to be a pillar of the community, and a friend to all who seek your services.
The following residents of Twillford send letters of personal commendation to our Office.
Prudence Mortimer, for your impeccable refinement and discretion, and for your affection,
Lady Priya Summer, for your passionate artistic sensibilities, and your caring spirit,
Duchess Marie Summer, for your ambition, grace, and unwavering friendship,
Edith Swan, for your theatrical flair, tireless work ethic, and great compassion,
Alice Wren, for your powerful imagination, your understanding, and your sweet temperament,
Fiona Trussard, for your services in promoting her business, and for your boundless curiosity regarding her personal life,
Lady Vivian Duskbourne, for your cunning intelligence and obliging nature,
Dorothy Parker, for your patience, enthusiasm, and immense kindness,
Rosalind Page, for seeing her when no one else did.

Based on these commendations, and our own adora-tion of your work, it is our profound pleasure to bestow upon you the title of Knight of the Realm. We offer our congratulations, and trust you know that this honour could not be more deserved.

You shall be required to present yourself forthwith at the Royal Palace for the occasion of the Knighthood Ceremony. Please attend attired in a dress befitting of the occasion, and demonstrative of your skill as the best dressmaker of Hemstitch.
With great expectation and the fullest trust,

One would think the sister of a duke might partake of less controversial occupations, but Lady Priya Summer never ceases to eschew convention. Her latest exhibition of paintings was unveiled at the Twillford Gallery this week, and is sure to affirm her burgeoning reputation as a pioneer of the floralescent movement…and as a disreputable woman within mannered society.

Truth be told, there is something rather febrile in the Lady’s brushstrokes, an unmistakeable and volatile passion present even in the smallest details. One cannot imagine any future husband would approve of such public indiscretion; such wanton expression of feeling verges upon the indecent.

Nevertheless, one must admire—nay envy—the loveliness of the Lady’s eveningwear. Lady Priya arrived in a truly resplendent dress, appearing like the figure from a romantic ballad in her {0} {1}, and prompting wistful sighs from jealous onlookers.
The exhibition proved well-attended too, as if full half the town suddenly fancied themselves veritable connoisseurs of the arts.

Adora Thimblethread, Twillford’s newfound athletic extraordinaire, was present, and set out to prove herself not only physically adroit but surpassingly cultured. She wore a daring ensemble quite unlike the staid fashions favoured by the milieu.

Adora Thimblethread, Twillford’s newfound athletic extraordinaire, was present, and attempted to prove herself not only physically adroit but knowledgeable of the arts. However, she could hardly be credited with aesthetic expertise when she consented to wearing that bizarre and unflattering a dress.

Certainly, she succeeded in turning many a head. In particular, Lady Vivian Duskbourne, herself immaculately attired in sultry eveningwear, watched the young sportswoman with an intemperate and uncivil intensity. One wonders whether Lady Vivian coveted the attention Miss Adora received? Indeed, she seemed on the verge of hissing like a territorial cat.

Certainly, she succeeded in turning many a head. In particular, Lady Vivian Duskbourne, herself attired in decidedly underwhelming eveningwear, watched the young sportswoman with an intemperate and uncivil intensity. One wonders whether Lady Vivian coveted the attention Miss Adora received? Indeed, she seemed on the verge of hissing like a territorial cat.

For months, the air of the town has swirled with fearful rumours regarding the mysterious disappearance of Princess Sophie Vasar. A week past, such speculation was finally put to rest — the royal palace joyfully pronounced that the Princess had been found unharmed, and that her ascendance to the throne would proceed unimpeded.

One was relieved to hear of this news, and thrilled for the opportunity to attend the coronation of Hemstitch’s new monarch. In truth, one knows little of the young ruler. Her public appearances have been few, and, as per royal tradition, Princess Sophie has always remained masked and veiled before her polity. Is it any surprise, then, for her to be the object of intense curiosity?

Well, one still has not beheld her face, but in every other respect, one finds Princess Sophie worthy of her new throne. Her coronation was both stately and spectacular, and the Princess addressed those in attendance with a profound, articulate, and compassionate intelligence. One would vouch that she shall not be found wanting, nor disappoint her people.

It goes without saying that her dress was magnificent. Description shall do it no justice; her vestments seemed almost to possess a mystical power. The Princess veritably glowed as she was crowned Queen.

While most could not hope to hold a candle before such radiance, Marie Laroche — Twillford’s new Duchess and renowned diplomat — certainly made a valiant showing. One was pleased to see her in attendance with her husband. Our Diplomat Duchess has a refinement and style that few can aspire to emulate, and which shall be sorely missed as she ventures forth to represent the nation’s interests in Cambric. One hopes she shall not remain abroad too long.
One did note, in passing, the strange absence of the Duke’s sister. Lady Priya Summer would ordinarily be expected to attend such an important event, and one wonders what may afflict her.
Surely no one in Twillford has failed to hear the news, but one is nevertheless compelled to proclaim it — the Duke has finally wed his Duchess!

Undoubtedly, the proposal came as the most exciting revelation of the season. The town had been abuzz with rumours for weeks, but the confirmation of Duke Hassan’s engagement to Marie Laroche produced a heretofore unrivalled fracas.
This wedding, it was agreed, would be surpassingly spectacular. The décor, the food, the fashion? Many a lady grew overwhelmed at the mere imagining of such glorious splendour.

And yet the real event still surpassed all expectations. Miss Marie’s wedding dress was radiant. Resplendent! Remarkable! Words fail one, but the {0} gown was quite possibly the finest article of clothing one has ever had the privilege to look upon. Miss Marie herself appeared the very picture of regal grace, and Duke Hassan bore the mildly baffled expression of a man encountering his own personal miracle.
Lady Priya Summer, herself attired in a perfectly lovely dress befitting her position as Maid of Honour, seemed well-pleased of this union. The sister of the Duke was in high spirits.

Lady Priya Summer, herself attired in a highly questionable dress that one shall not remark upon further in light of the happy occasion, seemed well-pleased of this union. The sister of the Duke was in high spirits.
That is, at least until the arrival of Prudence Mortimer.

While it cannot be said that Miss Prudence ever possessed an aversion to scandal, her arrival at the wedding beggared the question of whether she had, in fact, lost her mind entirely. Bad enough to show her face in such an obvious state of ill-humour and bitter animosity—all knew she coveted the Duke’s hand for herself—but to comport herself in such an outrageous dress? Beyond the pale!

Her disgraceful appearance dragged the Mortimer name into the mud of disrepute. Did she think to tempt the Duke at the very altar with her salacious display? Thankfully, Lady Priya acted swiftly, and removed the recalcitrant hussy from the ceremony afore either the Duke or his bride witnessed any rude antics.
One can only imagine that is the last we shall see of Prudence Mortimer in polite company! Good riddance, one says.

A Duke’s funeral, one would presume, should be a sombre and sober occasion. The laying-to-rest of our late Duke Donovan Summer, however, proved such presumptions flawed — Twillford society, by and large, evinced a festive comportment more typically reserved for audiences of circus shows.

Certainly, none of the young ladies in attendance appeared particularly grieved at the loss of Duke Donovan. Although eyes were dutifully dabbed, and sighs were solemnly soughed, the maidenly contingent seemed much more preoccupied with the deceased’s handsome heir.
Duke Hassan Summer is, after all, now conspicuously in want of a Duchess.
Suffice to say, he shan’t suffer any dearth of applications for that role. Before his uncle’s coffin had even reached the soil, the new Duke found himself positively beset with young ladies.

Foremost amongst the aspirants was Prudence Mortimer, who arrived garbed in the most outrageous {0} dress. While she undoubtedly drew the Duke’s notice, it is unclear if her flagrant flouting of decorum won her any measure of his affection. Certainly, his relations were far from impressed by Miss Prudence’s antics. Lady Priya Summer, garbed in {1}, was visibly incensed. Had she suffered a hair more provocation, one wonders whether Lady Priya and Miss Prudence might have come to physical blows, thereby transforming an already risible funeral into an outright farce.

In stark contrast to the scandalous attire of Miss Prudence, however, was the garb of one Marie Laroche. Miss Marie wore a fine, sensible, and most flattering dress, and was seen in serious conversation with Duke Hassan — much to the envy and dismay of the lace-swaddled masses. One would dearly love to know the name of her dressmaker!

As if the day had not seen sufficient fashion faux pas, the arrival of one Marie Laroche caused yet another stir. One wonders whether Miss Marie and Miss Prudence frequent the same dressmaker’s shop, and, if so, how quickly such a dismal institution might be shuttered for the good of society.

It is well understood by learnéd minds that moderate physical exertion is of tremendous import to the balancing of the bodily humours. Thus, it is only proper that a healthy lady might be permitted to partake of a stimulating stroll.

It likewise follows that a pleasant environ can only enhance the benefits of such exercise. The breathing of good vapours, and the imbuement of lovely sights and sounds, is certain to have a restorative influence, brightening the eyes and lifting the spirits. As such, the re-opening of the Twillford Hedge Maze last week is indubitably a cause for celebration.

Many enterprising women have already availed themselves of the opportunity to walk the tidy hedgerows. Amongst their number was Alice Wren, dressed splendidly for the occasion. Her white gown was simply picturesque, and much coveted by other walkers.
However, by her expression, she was rather put out by something — one wonders whether she encountered a disappointment, perhaps of a romantic nature.

Many fine ladies have already availed themselves of the opportunity to walk the tidy hedgerows. Amongst their number was Alice Wren, who, as is her apparent wont, dressed like a ghastly apparition. One can only assume she thought that the labyrinth’s function might be enhanced should the hedge maze be haunted.

But stranger things were afoot than Miss Alice. Dorothy Parker, Twillford’s ardent birder, was sighted in the most curious of dresses — she seemed, by her attire and posture, to be intent on imitating shrubbery.

Miss Parker might even have succeeded in this venture, were she not accompanied by Fiona Trussard. Mrs Fiona, in contrast to her companion, wore an exceedingly loud dress that immediately drew the attention of everyone within the vicinity.

She, being impossible to miss, and Miss Dorothy, being quite difficult to see, made for a most odd pairing. Indeed, Miss Dorothy seemed rather cross about the discrepancy. One heard her exclaim, “But, Fiona, how shall we ever uncover a tryst under these conditions?!” to which Mrs Fiona replied, “I do not care to uncover a tryst,” to which Miss Dorothy replied, “But I subsist on trysts!” to which Mrs Fiona replied with a recommendation for a dietary adjustment, and the offer of a discount on courgettes.

Miss Parker might even have succeeded in this venture, were she not accompanied by Fiona Trussard. Mrs Fiona seemed intent on making as much noise as possible while moving through the maze, thereby drawing the attention of everyone within the vicinity.

Thus Mrs Fiona, being impossible to miss, and Miss Dorothy, being quite difficult to see, made for a most odd pairing. Indeed, Miss Dorothy seemed rather cross about the situation. One heard her exclaim, “But, Fiona, how shall we ever uncover a tryst under these conditions?!” to which Mrs Fiona replied, “I do not care to uncover a tryst,” to which Miss Dorothy replied, “But I subsist on trysts!” to which Mrs Fiona replied with a recommendation for a dietary adjustment, and the offer of a discount on courgettes.

Industry and commerce are scarcely one’s favourite objects of conversation, both involving, one would assume, an unseemly abundance of tiresome mathematics. Nevertheless, the boisterous bustle of trade at this month’s Market Fair proved surprisingly invigorating.

A great variety of foodstuffs were available for sampling and sale. Many a stall featured a youth sporting a dolorous expression and a tray of cut fruits. Here, one might be provisioned with a dear little fork, and permitted to nibble upon a slice of strawberry or a segment of satsuma. Delightful! A great inducement to shop! One approves most heartily of this new practice.

One would further assert that no stall at the fair was better provisioned than that belonging to Fiona Trussard. While Mrs Fiona is new to Twillford, one ardently hopes she never departs. Her turnips are to die for, her cabbages beyond compare.

She is also to be commended for her bold instinct for fashion. Truly, who would have thought to promote one’s wares with one’s own dress? These modern promotional methodologies are most ingenious. Mrs Fiona’s dress looked every part as delectable as her vegetables.

Assisting Mrs Fiona was amateur ornithologist Dorothy Parker and the esteemed Edith Swan. Mrs Edith took a wondrous page from Mrs Fiona’s book, and wore a dress that transformed her into the very picture of a luscious carrot. Dazzled as one was, one could not help but to leave Mrs Fiona’s stall with a cornucopia of vegetable riches.

Assisting Mrs Fiona was amateur ornithologist Dorothy Parker and the esteemed Edith Swan. However, Mrs Swan seemed rather removed from her bygone days of operatic glamour — one wonders what possessed her to wear such a terrible {0} garment. Indeed, Mrs Fiona appeared none too pleased by the choice. One rather suspects it drove off potential customers!
One is given to understand that people may possess varied proclivities, but, for the life of one, one cannot comprehend an obsession with domestic animals that would result in a Pet Show.

Does one wish to gaze upon another dreary terrier, or saturnine budgerigar, or quiversome rabbit? No. No, one does not care one jot for such beasts. They BORE one. One is not even permitted to pet them!
What, one asks, is the point of a pet show without any petting?
However, as one has obligingly already stated, people possess varied proclivities, and some, doubtless, appreciate the opportunity to sit within a small hall and smell the animals.

This year’s Pet Show saw a diverse range of contestants. Dorothy Parker, a regular winner of the event, saw fit to compete with a shy pigeon named Montgomery. It was evident that the attractive young bird possessed a great deal of love and trust for Miss Dorothy. Upon taking fright at the sight of the judging panel, he immediately burrowed into her quilt-like patchwork dress, and would not be coaxed out despite the inducements of seeds and berries.

The standard of dress at the event likewise left much to be desired. While Dorothy Parker sported a fine young bird named Montgomery, her own attire seemed completely unsuited to the occasion, and appeared, in fact, to upset many of the other animals. One wonders whether this visual sabotage was her intention.

Mrs Fiona Trussard ultimately cinched victory alongside her handsome ox, Alphonse. Mrs Fiona, ordinarily a most sensible and stoic woman, appeared singularly moved by this win. She hugged Alphonse very tightly, apparently close to tears. Alphonse bore these affections with great temperance, and the pair looked most charming as they collected the trophy.

Mrs Fiona Trussard ultimately cinched victory alongside her handsome ox, Alphonse. Mrs Fiona, ordinarily a most sensible and stoic woman, appeared singularly moved by this win. She hugged Alphonse very tightly, apparently close to tears. Alphonse bore these affections with great temperance.

The aesthetic impression of their victory was slightly marred by Mrs Fiona’s incomprehensible choice of dress. Perhaps her domestic animals had fouled every other garment in her wardrobe, that she was reduced to such an ugly {0} frock.

One finds oneself dwelling, in recent days, on the joy of a kept secret. One’s reader might think, “why, is this not antithetical to one’s habitual purpose, when one’s writing fearlessly seeks to illuminate and uncover?” To which one might humbly rejoin that one can contain multitudes.

Besides which, what thrill does gossip possess if it is known by all? A happy secret, a private covenant, transforms one into a link within a chain — enjoins one to a small and precious community of fellow confidence-holders. One is made rarefied by privileged knowledge, and lessened by its disclosure.
So, contrary to one’s nature, one shall not be careless with this particular secret.

One will only say—with the utmost circumspection!—that one has been given cause to regret one’s unkind treatment of Miss Prudence Mortimer. One wishes her to know that one is sorry for one’s harsh words, and gladdened of her newfound happiness. One trusts her days shall henceforth be garlanded with flowers.

One is likewise pleased to hear of the much-improved spirits of the town’s finest painter, Lady Priya Summer. One hopes that she perceives the number of residents who worried after her health, and understands that Twillford is dimmed in the absence of her colour and light. One trusts that her nights shall henceforth be illuminated by starshine.

One shall stay one’s pen here, and wish one’s reader well until the delivery of our next dispatch. Until then, may we all celebrate the flowers and the stars, and the small secret miracles that blossom unseen around us.

A fine sporting performance is a marvellous sight to behold, while a poor one nonetheless supplies bountiful amusement. Therefore, the annual Twillford Woman’s Sporting Day Contest consistently provides cause for good cheer\: if one does not witness a feat of athletic brilliance, one is at least assured the pleasure of a spectacular failure.
This year’s field did not disappoint. While there was, admittedly, a surplus of middling performers, the contest also boasted unexpected jewels of both bravura and ineptitude.

Who would have credited it? It transpires that Prudence Mortimer is a near-unparalleled sportswoman. More commonly witnessed partaking in social teas and extolling the virtues of upright posture, if Miss Prudence’s participation came as a surprise, her aptitude proved an outright shock. Where has the lady developed her seemingly indefatigable endurance? From whence came her lithe strength and agility?

Observing Miss Prudence, many an enraptured lady found themselves in sudden need of a silk fan — as though the heat of her exertions were transmitted by an intangible conduit. A most curious phenomenon.

However, when it seemed all but certain that Miss Prudence would win the day, a mysterious new competitor entered the field. Bearing the unusual name of ‘Adora Thimblethread’ and gorgeously dressed for the occasion, the young woman moved with singular focus and determination as she decimated the competition. What a vision of well-dressed athleticism!

Against such fierce competitors, poor Alice Wren stood little chance of prevailing. Swiftly, it became apparent that Miss Alice was not made for speed, stamina, or strength. One might hazard that she was instead made, primarily, for tripping over minor obstacles and taking fright at loud noises.

Nevertheless, Miss Alice seemed in high spirits, and most committed to the contest. While she might have placed last of all the participants, she did so in excellent style. Her {0} dress was perhaps the loveliest of the day.

Although Miss Alice is to be commended for her commitment to participation, she was doomed to place last in every event. One wonders whether her choice of dress might have compounded her loss — she wore a {0} ensemble that looked most hideous. One can only imagine she found such a dress dispiriting.
Ah, springtime! The promise of blooming flowers, frolicking lambs, and burgeoning romance. Is there any better season for gossip? One thinks not!

And oh, the Spring Fete! After a long winter and a dearth of parties, one is left near giddy from the sheer abundance of glamour and delight. All the ladies turn out in their fresh gowns, glittering and gay, and infect the very air with good cheer.

Even Prudence Mortimer, Twillford’s eternal wellspring of spectacle, arrived at the Fete looking quite beautiful. Her floral dress may have been a departure from her usual fashions, but it suited her tremendously well.

Perhaps it was simply happiness that transformed the lady. Miss Prudence gained a veritable glow while in conversation with Lady Priya Summer, expounding at length on her enthusiasm for their future sororal relationship. Lady Priya appeared more than a little aggravated at this juncture, but one suspects Miss Prudence did not notice.

That is not to say that the apparel of all ladies was equally becoming. Prudence Mortimer, Twillford’s eternal wellspring of spectacle, wore a {0} dress that could best be described as a challenge to the very notions of beauty, temperance, and good taste. Any sensible woman would have fired her dressmaker, and furthermore set fire to that dress.

Nevertheless, Miss Prudence seemed in high spirits. She made many a glowing allusion to her apparently inevitable upcoming matrimony, and to how many chaise lounges she expects the Duke might possess. (Her estimates are upwards of thirty-four.)

However, the jewel of the evening was undoubtedly Marie Laroche. Her dress was marvellous, and the very essence of springtime romantic grace. None could take their eyes off the young lady; a palpable hush fell over the hall when she walked through the doors.
If his stupefied expression at the sight of Miss Marie was any indication, one might be led to suspect that Duke Hassan shan’t remain unattached for very much longer…

In the search of print-worthy truths, one is frequently required to go to unusual lengths and partake of unconventional methods. Thus, one might, for example, find oneself crouched within a thorn bush in the middle of the night, peering between the leaves to observe the attendees of a stargazing party.

One is saying, in brief, that such an exercise is very cold, dim, and unpleasant, and entirely too full of insects (some of which bite one!) and one trusts that one’s reader greatly appreciates all that one does for the sake of acquiring interesting gossip for their gentle perusal.
While it is challenging to observe the finer points of dress and decorum under such conditions, one did see a great deal of activity upon the darkened hillside.

Adora Thimblethread traipsed past in a mysterious and most attractive dress, looking every bit like a moon maiden of mythology. Her expression struck one as distant and contemplative; one wonders what might have troubled her.
Adora Thimblethread traipsed past, garbed in an awful frock she surely anticipated would never be seen by another living soul. Alas, Miss Adora. One saw you. One wondered at your frame of mind.

Shortly thereafter, Lady Vivian Duskbourne passed by one’s bush. A dreadfully frightening sight! While the lady certainly wore a becoming dress, she possessed a most fearsome energy and a mien that betokened imminent violence. One stayed very still and very quiet until one was very sure that Lady Vivian had departed.

After such a shock, one contemplated departing for home. (One had already suffered enough, one thought.) But as one was on the verge of committing to such a course, Prudence Mortimer happened by. As Miss Prudence is inevitably one’s surest source of scandal, one was persuaded to remain embushed.

Miss Prudence took a short, solitary stroll, and then sat upon a flat rock just below the summit of the hill. She seemed immensely melancholy…as well a disreputable hussy should! One can report that her posture was not remotely up to standard.

One was once again on the verge of departing (for watching Miss Prudence sit was less engaging than one had hoped, and one was also quite sure that something unwholesome had crawled into one’s shoe) when one sighted Lady Priya Summer climbing the hill.

Poor Lady Priya did not notice Miss Prudence until she was almost upon the wretch. After Miss Prudence’s behaviour at the Duke’s wedding, one would have assumed Lady Priya would want nothing to do with such a person. Thus one was rather surprised when the good Lady joined Miss Prudence upon her flat rock. The pair spoke for a very long time, but one could not hear their correspondence from one’s vantage.
All one can report is that, when Miss Prudence finally left the rock, Lady Priya appeared tremendously hurt.

What could be more romantic, more thrilling, more glamorous, than a masquerade? A costumed soiree permits the free expression of one’s creativity, grants permission for a degree of extravagance and whimsy ill-suited to the more humdrum party.
That is why, one believes, the Summer Ball is the most wonderful night of the social calendar.

It is of no import that the masks of the revellers do little to conceal their identities. A painted beak or horn cannot obscure, for example, Miss Rita’s distinctive freckling or Mr Benjamin’s telltale odour. However, so long as participants are willing to pretend at ignorance, the magic of the game endures.
Forgive one, then, for the laying aside of this cherished pretence, but one must—one simply must!—write of the gown of Miss Alice Wren.

In the past, one has dwelt on Miss Alice’s various ineptitudes, primarily those of a physical nature. And yet, at the Ball, she exhibited no trace of clumsiness, no sign of uncertainty, confusion, or apprehension. Miss Alice, instead, exuded a self-assurance and poise that commanded the attention of the entire room. Her raven-themed costume was every part as glossy and darkly magnificent as one might have hoped. Certainly, it was the most gorgeous dress of any lady in attendance.
Further, Miss Alice seemed so content within herself, so enviably confident and unapologetic. One is divided between describing her demeanour as fearless or simply…settled.
Regardless, it attracted many admirers that evening. One ventures that this new confidence shall win Miss Alice a plenitude of friends, and one finds oneself unexpectedly pleased on her behalf.
Adora wants an avant-garde dress for Priya's exhibition.
I have no idea what you are talking about. My name is Adora Thimblethread — which is a perfectly normal and not at all unusual name.
…you have a terrible sense of humour.
Nevertheless, I would like us to be friends. I want to get to know everyone in Twillford better!
Ever since the Women’s Sporting Day Contest, I’ve felt…observed.
It feels as though someone is watching me from the shadows.
Ahh, stop! I can’t handle ghost stories.
A fell force lurks in the darkness.
It creeps toward the dressmaker’s shop, fangs gleaming and wet—
I’ll fix it! I promise I can do better! Please don’t think I—
That wasn’t very nice, but I concede I had it coming.
You really are that scared of disappointing other people?
No one loves a disappointment. I don’t want people to look at me and see a waste.
